purpose: Document microeconomic, domestic macroeconomic, global and corporate-ownership channels in the daily-life benchmark story. No numerical causal decomposition without comparable data and identification.
rules: Keep the household expenditure benchmark separate from price inflation, forecasts and policy rates.
Distinguish published observations, regulatory allegations, estimates and unknown impacts.
No company or wealthy individual is assigned an individual cost premium without outcome evidence.
A ZIP is not a business service territory or a politician's district; national relationships do not imply local business activity.
Government forecasts and indexes must display date, unit, geography, uncertainty and original source.

signals.name: U.S. consumer prices
signals.explain: Overall CPI-U price increase; not a household spending change.
signals.limits: Price indices do not assign causes to companies or policies.

signals.name: Food-at-home prices
signals.explain: Prices of groceries within the CPI basket.
signals.limits: Not the change in grocery outlays or a local store's prices.

signals.name: U.S. energy prices
signals.explain: CPI energy index over 12 months, reflecting multiple types of energy.
signals.limits: Not a direct change in local gas, electricity or utility bills.

signals.name: Gasoline prices
signals.limits: Price changes vary by region and grade; total gasoline spending also depends on mileage.

signals.name: U.S. shelter prices
signals.explain: CPI shelter component change including rent and owners' equivalent rent.
signals.limits: Not current asking rent in any ZIP.

signals.name: U.S. medical care services
signals.explain: CPI medical care services component change.
signals.limits: Not an individual's premium, patient balance or provider quote.

signals.name: Federal funds target
signals.explain: Short-term policy-rate target; influences many financial conditions.
signals.limits: Not a mortgage, auto-loan or government borrowing interest rate.

signals.name: Global economic growth
signals.explain: IMF forecast for 2026 real world GDP growth.
signals.limits: A forecast, not a current price change or local economic finding.

signals.name: Global headline inflation
signals.explain: IMF forecast of global inflation across country indexes.
signals.limits: Not directly comparable with a U.S. household's grocery or energy inflation.

signals.name: World energy commodities
signals.explain: World Bank projected year-over-year energy commodity price increase.
signals.limits: NOT the change in household bills; wholesale shocks pass through unevenly.

signals.name: World food commodities
signals.explain: World Bank projected food commodity price increase.
signals.limits: International food commodities are not a U.S. retail grocery-price index.

mechanisms: Domestic financing
Interest rates and construction credit can change new-housing supply and borrowing costs; this does not immediately reprice fixed mortgages.
International materials and capital
Global fuel, imported building inputs and international capital may affect development costs and housing demand; effects depend on the local market.
housing.firm: Landlords, institutional investors, developers, lenders and major shareholders can influence supply, lease terms, acquisitions and pricing. Only the cited case records can establish particular actions.

mechanisms: Domestic inflation and distribution
Farming, processing, wages, freight and retailer margins contribute differently to grocery prices; food CPI tracks measured retail price changes, not their causes.
International food and fuel
Conflict, trade restrictions, harvest disruption, and global energy prices can affect imported goods and domestic production costs, with imperfect pass-through.
groceries.firm: Supermarkets, processors, wholesalers and platforms set markups, negotiate procurement, and choose package sizes; shareholders can influence strategy but do not automatically set shelf prices.

mechanisms: U.S. energy and approved rates
Fuel markets and regulated delivery investment can alter energy prices; a broad CPI energy index cannot substitute for a utility bill.
International oil and gas
World commodity shocks can pass through to gasoline, heating fuels and electricity where relevant, mediated by contracts, generation mix, and regulation.
energy.firm: Major energy producers, utilities, infrastructure owners and investors influence investment and market supply; actual rate-setting depends on regulators and tariffs.

mechanisms: Domestic reimbursement and capacity
Hospital staffing, insurer negotiation, plan design and financing may affect payments and access; broad medical CPI is not a premium.
International supplies and manufacturing
Imported ingredients, medical devices, global shipping and exchange rates can affect procurement costs, though reimbursement rules and contracts mediate patient effects.
health.firm: Insurers, hospitals, pharmacy benefit managers, drug manufacturers and private-equity owners can influence contracts and care economics; measured price effects depend on the specific study.

mechanisms: Wages vs purchasing power
Inflation, borrowing rates and domestic demand can affect real earnings and hiring; nominal pay is not the same as purchasing power.
Trade and global demand
Foreign demand, import competition, exchange rates and supply-chain disruptions can affect industries and jobs unevenly.
work.firm: Large employers, controlling shareholders and investors set investment, staffing and compensation policies within labor and competition law; local employer concentration may matter.

mechanisms: Childcare labor and finance
Staffing, state funding, borrowing and local capacity influence childcare fees; school expenditure and private childcare prices are different.
International costs
Fuel, imported supplies and food costs can affect provider budgets, but labor and enrollment often dominate local care fees.
schools.firm: Childcare chains, private-equity shareholders, real-estate owners and public education vendors can influence fees and operating choices; verify local provider and brand links.

mechanisms: U.S. fuel, auto finance and insurance
Gasoline prices and interest rates change parts of travel cost; car insurance and transit depend on separate factors.
Global oil and automotive supply
International crude supply, tariffs, shipping and auto components can affect fuel and vehicle prices, depending on exposure and inventories.
transport.firm: Oil producers, vehicle makers, insurers, dealers, transit operators, platforms and financiers influence costs through supply, contracts and pricing decisions.

mechanisms: Public budgets and financing
Government wages, debt financing, property assessments and procurement influence public-service costs; federal rates are not local tax rates.
International inputs and fiscal risk
Imported infrastructure materials, fuel and global borrowing conditions can change project costs, with contract and tax timing delays.
public-services.firm: Government contractors and their owners may receive awards, lobby or donate; contract terms and documented decisions are required before alleging a return or price effect.

mechanisms: Domestic decisions
Monetary, fiscal, tax, zoning and competition policy have distinct effects and timelines; an official decision is not proof of a particular local price impact.
International policy and shocks
Trade negotiations, sanctions, geopolitical conflicts, commodity supply and exchange rates can change policy trade-offs and household costs.
representation.firm: Large donors, business groups and wealthy investors may finance advocacy and campaigns. Disclosures document payments and recipients; they do not prove policies were purchased.

corporate.fallback: No verified company-specific price effect for this category. Investigate local presence, pricing, ownership structure and financing independently.
